claim: Most craniofacial structures originate from the vertebrate-specific neural crest cells except in the dorsal portion of the head, where they arise from cranial mesoderm.
source: Most craniofacial structures originate from the vertebrate-specific neural crest cells except in the dorsal portion of the head, where they arise from cranial mesoderm.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the developmental origins of craniofacial structures, presented as background information in the abstract.

claim: Bipotent progenitors expressing Myf5 give rise to both muscle and juxtaposed connective tissue.
source: Here, using multiple lineage-tracing strategies combined with single cell RNAseq and in situ analyses, we identify bipotent progenitors expressing Myf5 (an upstream regulator of myogenic fate) that give rise to both muscle and juxtaposed connective tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including lineage tracing, scRNAseq, and in situ analyses as stated in the abstract.

claim: Following bifurcation, muscle and connective tissue cells retain complementary signalling features and maintain spatial proximity.
source: Following this bifurcation, muscle and connective tissue cells retain complementary signalling features and maintain spatial proximity.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from the study presented in the abstract.

claim: Disrupting myogenic identity shifts muscle progenitors to a connective tissue fate.
source: Disrupting myogenic identity shifts muscle progenitors to a connective tissue fate.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental manipulation described in the abstract.

claim: The emergence of Myf5-derived connective tissue is associated with the activity of several transcription factors, including Foxp2.
source: The emergence of Myf5-derived connective tissue is associated with the activity of several transcription factors, including Foxp2.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from the study presented in the abstract.

claim: The bifurcation in cell fate was not observed in craniofacial regions that are colonised by neural crest cells.
source: Interestingly, this unexpected bifurcation in cell fate was not observed in craniofacial regions that are colonised by neural crest cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from the study presented in the abstract.

claim: An ancestral bi-fated program gives rise to muscle and connective tissue cells in skeletal muscles that are deprived of neural crest cells.
source: Therefore, we propose that an ancestral bi-fated program gives rise to muscle and connective tissue cells in skeletal muscles that are deprived of neural crest cells.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings presented in the abstract.

claim: The majority of muscle-associated connective tissues in the head is derived from cranial neural crest cells.
source: The majority of muscle-associated connective tissues in the head is derived from cranial neural crest cells (NCCs), an embryonic cell population that contributes to most of the structural components of the 'new head', a vertebrate innovation (Le Douarin and Kalcheim, 1999; Gans and Northcutt, 1983; Grenier et al., 2009; Heude et al., 2018; Noden and Trainor, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Extraocular, laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles contain mesenchyme that is mesoderm-derived in their dorso-medial component, whereas the remaining muscle mass is embedded in mesenchyme that is neural crest-derived.
source: Recently, the extent of this contribution was redefined in muscles derived from cranial mesoderm, including extraocular (EOM), laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles (Comai et al., 2020; Grimaldi et al., 2015; Heude et al., 2018; Kuroda et al., 2021; Noden and Epstein, 2010). Interestingly, these muscles contain mesenchyme that is mesoderm-derived in their dorso-medial component, whereas the remaining muscle mass is embedded in mesenchyme that is neural crest-derived.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Paraxial somitic mesoderm gives rise to skeletal muscles and associated connective tissues along the trunk axis.
source: Along the trunk axis, paraxial somitic mesoderm gives rise to skeletal muscles and associated connective tissues (Burke and Nowicki, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The dermomyotome gives rise to several cell types including all skeletal muscles of the body, vasculature, tendons and bones.
source: Upon signals emanating from adjacent tissues, the dermomyotome (dorsal portion of the somite) undergoes an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and gives rise to several cell types including all skeletal muscles of the body, vasculature, tendons and bones (Ben-Yair and Kalcheim, 2008; Christ et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cardiopharyngeal mesoderm has cardiovascular potential, which manifests in the embryo as regions of clonally related cardiac and craniofacial skeletal muscles.
source: Moreover, cardiopharyngeal mesoderm, which constitutes the major portion of cranial mesoderm, has cardiovascular potential, which manifests in the embryo as regions of clonally related cardiac and craniofacial skeletal muscles (Diogo et al., 2015; Swedlund and Lescroart, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cardiopharyngeal mesoderm was shown to give rise to connective tissues in the mammalian pharynx.
source: While cardiopharyngeal mesoderm was shown to give rise to connective tissues in the mammalian pharynx, the extent of its contribution to other craniofacial muscles in general has not been fully addressed (Adachi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A large portion of cells obtained by Mesp1Cre/+;Rosa26mTmG/+ lineage tracing at E10.5 segregated as individual clusters expressing markers of adipogenic, chondrogenic, sclerotomal, endothelial, and cardiovascular lineages as well as the foregut and primitive lung mesenchyme.
source: After removal of doublets and lower quality cells (see Materials and methods), a large portion of the cells obtained by Mesp1Cre/+;Rosa26mTmG/+ lineage tracing segregated as individual clusters expressing markers of adipogenic, chondrogenic, sclerotomal, endothelial, and cardiovascular lineages as well as the foregut and primitive lung mesenchyme (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: About half of the supposedly myogenic cells exhibited a connective tissue signature, including a strong bias toward Prrx1, Col1a1, and Twist1.
source: Surprisingly, about half of the supposedly myogenic cells exhibited a connective tissue signature, including a strong bias toward Prrx1, a marker of lateral plate mesoderm (Durland et al., 2008), Col1a1, a major extracellular matrix component of connective tissue cells (De Micheli et al., 2020), and Twist1, a key determinant for the mesenchymal properties of cranial mesoderm (Bildsoe et al., 2016; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1F and citations to previous literature.

claim: Pdgfra expression was robustly anticorrelated with the expression of its ligand Pdgfa and associated with non-myogenic genes.
source: Furthermore, the expression of Pdgfra, a well-defined marker of stromal cells (Farahani and Xaymardan, 2015), was robustly anticorrelated with the expression of its ligand Pdgfa and associated with non-myogenic genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pdgfa was correlated with a myogenic cell state.
source: Conversely, Pdgfa, was correlated with a myogenic cell state (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1F and supplementary figures.

claim: Myogenic Pdgfa expression was shown to promote adjacent sclerotomal cells to adopt a rib cartilage fate.
source: Of note, myogenic Pdgfa expression was shown to promote adjacent sclerotomal cells to adopt a rib cartilage fate (Tallquist et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RNA velocity-inferred trajectories suggested that Myf5+ cells from the myogenic compartment contributed to non-myogenic cells.
source: Notably, RNA velocity-inferred trajectories suggested that Myf5+ cells from the myogenic compartment contributed to non-myogenic cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Top transcribed driver genes in anterior somites included Foxp1, Meox2, Meis1, Twist2, Fap, Pdgfra, Prrx1, and Pcolce, which are associated with fibrosis and connective tissue development.
source: Top transcribed driver genes included Foxp1 (Shao and Wei, 2018), Meox2 (Noizet et al., 2016), Meis1 (López-Delgado et al., 2020), Twist2 (Franco et al., 2009), Fap (Puré and Blomberg, 2018), Pdgfra (Tallquist et al., 2000), Prrx1 (Leavitt et al., 2020), and Pcolce (Bildsoe et al., 2016; Figure 2C), which are associated with fibrosis and connective tissue development.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA velocity driver gene analysis shown in Figure 2C and citations to previous literature.

claim: Pdgfra appeared as a driver gene and was activated along the inferred trajectory, whereas Pdgfa expression decreased rapidly.
source: Interestingly, we noted that Pdgfra appeared as a driver gene and was activated along this inferred trajectory, whereas Pdgfa expression decreased rapidly (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: RNA velocity analysis for anterior somite mesodermal progenitors showed that Myf5+/Pdgfa+ cells shifted toward a non-myogenic fate, which includes the downregulation of Myf5 and Pdgfa and the activation of Pdgfra expression.
source: Taken together, RNA velocity analysis for anterior somite mesodermal progenitors showed that Myf5+/Pdgfa+ cells shifted toward a non-myogenic fate, which includes the downregulation of Myf5 and Pdgfa and the activation of Pdgfra expression (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is a summary of RNA velocity analysis findings shown in Figure 2E.

claim: GFP+ TOM+ double-positive cells were observed in regions of EOM, laryngeal and upper back muscles that are partially or fully deprived of neural crest at E14.5.
source: Notably, we observed GFP+ TOM+ double-positive cells in regions of EOM, laryngeal and upper back muscles that are partially or fully deprived of neural crest (Adachi et al., 2020; Comai et al., 2020; Heude et al., 2018; Figure 3A–C').
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A-C' and citations to previous literature.

claim: No double-positive cells were detected in muscles that are fully embedded in neural crest derived mesenchyme such as mandibular and tongue muscles.
source: Conversely, no double-positive cells were detected in muscles that are fully embedded in neural crest derived mesenchyme such as mandibular and tongue muscles (Heude et al., 2018; Figure 3D–E').
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D-E' and a citation to previous literature.

claim: GFP+ cells that expressed Myf5 (β-gal+) were exclusively present in Mesp1-derived domains and absent from the Wnt1 lineage at E13.5.
source: Using Wnt1Cre/+; Rosa26mTmG/+; Myf5nlacZ/+ (NCC tracing with Wnt1) and Mesp1Cre/+;Rosa26mTmG/+;Myf5nlacZ/+ (mesoderm tracing with Mesp1) at E13.5, we found that GFP+ cells that expressed Myf5 (β-gal+) were exclusively present in Mesp1-derived domains and absent from the Wnt1 lineage (Figure 3F–I').
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3F-I'.

claim: A medio-lateral gradient of Myf5-lineage contribution to EOM-associated connective tissues was observed by E14.5, and this was anticorrelated with the local contribution of neural crest cells to connective tissues.
source: As expected, we observed a medio-lateral gradient of Myf5-lineage contribution to EOM-associated connective tissues by E14.5, and this was anticorrelated with the local contribution of neural crest cells to connective tissues (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3J-K.

claim: Individual cells undergo a progressive switch from myogenic to non-myogenic gene expression along the inferred trajectories, where cells at the transition zone shut off the myogenic program and start activating fibrogenic genes.
source: This analysis revealed that individual cells undergo a progressive switch from myogenic to non-myogenic gene expression along the inferred trajectories, where cells at the transition zone shut off the myogenic program and start activating fibrogenic genes (Figure 4C heatmap).
evidence: This claim is supported by coexpression score analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cells exhibiting a mostly non-overlapping, complementary pattern of Pdgfa and Pdgfra transcripts within the Myf5-derived lineage were observed at E14.5, while retaining anatomical proximity.
source: In accordance with the scRNAseq analysis, we observed cells exhibiting a mostly non-overlapping, complementary pattern of Pdgfa and Pdgfra transcripts within the Myf5-derived lineage, while retaining anatomical proximity, even at later stages of EOM development.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data described in the text.

claim: Bmpr1b and Ephb1 were among the top 100 driver genes of the myogenic EOM compartment, suggesting that myogenic commitment is associated with upregulation of these kinase receptors in the EOM.
source: Notably, Bmpr1b and Ephb1 were among the top 100 driver genes of the myogenic EOM compartment, suggesting that myogenic commitment is associated with upregulation of these kinase receptors in the EOM (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by driver gene analysis shown in supplementary figures and Table 1.

claim: Bmp4 and Efnb1 were preferentially expressed in non-myogenic cells.
source: Strikingly, two of their respective ligands, Bmp4 and Efnb1, were preferentially expressed in non-myogenic cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis described in the text.

claim: Analysis of Bmp4 and Efnb1 expression patterns in E14.5 embryos by RNAscope validated complementary expression patterns in adjacent muscle and connective tissue domains.
source: Analysis of their expression patterns in E14.5 embryos by RNAscope validated these complementary expression patterns in adjacent muscle and connective tissue domains (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Myf5, Pitx1, Mef2a, and Six1 appeared among the top regulons in myogenic cells.
source: Notably, Myf5, Pitx1, Mef2a, and Six1, transcription factors known to be implicated in myogenic development (Buckingham and Rigby, 2014), appeared among the top regulons in myogenic cells
evidence: This claim is supported by SCENIC analysis and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Fli1, Ebf1, Ets1, Foxc1, Meis1, and Six2 constituted some of the highly active non-myogenic transcription factors.
source: whereas Fli1, Ebf1, Ets1, Foxc1, Meis1, and Six2, genes known for their involvement in adipogenic, vascular, mesenchymal and tendon development (Jimenez et al., 2007; López-Delgado et al., 2020; Noizet et al., 2016; Truong and Ben-David, 2000; Whitesell et al., 2019; Yamamoto-Shiraishi and Kuroiwa, 2013), constituted some of the highly active non-myogenic transcription factors (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by SCENIC analysis shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous literature.

claim: Scube1 was upregulated in the Pdgfra+ non-myogenic fraction of the EOM.
source: Accordingly, we found that Scube1, a gene known for its involvement in vasculature development, was upregulated in the Pdgfra+ non-myogenic fraction of the EOM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: RNAscope in situ hybridization confirmed that Scube1 was expressed at the level of the EOM medial attachment at E14.5.
source: RNAscope in situ hybridization confirmed these findings and showed that Scube1 was expressed at the level of the EOM medial attachment at E14.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Disruption of Myf5 activity led to a threefold increase in the proportion of non-myogenic Myf5-derived cells in the EOM region.
source: Notably, disruption of Myf5 activity led to a threefold increase in the proportion of non-myogenic Myf5-derived cells in this region (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data from Myf5 null embryos shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: No double-positive cells were found in the masseter, a muscle fully embedded in neural crest-derived connective tissue, even in the absence of Myf5.
source: In contrast, no double-positive cells were found in the masseter, a muscle fully embedded in neural crest-derived connective tissue, even in the absence of Myf5 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data from Myf5 null embryos shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Very few Pdgfra+ cells were found to be derived from Myod expressing cells in MyodiCre;Rosa26TdTomato/+;PdgfraH2BGFP/+ fetuses at E14.5.
source: In contrast, very few Pdgfra+ cells were found to be derived from Myod expressing cells in MyodiCre;Rosa26TdTomato/+;PdgfraH2BGFP/+ fetuses at E14.5, particularly in the EOM and the back muscles (about 3 and 1.5 cells per 100 μm2 of muscle, respectively)(Figure 5G, I, J).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5G, I, J.

claim: The masseter lacked Myod-derived connective tissue cells.
source: Accordingly, the masseter lacked Myod-derived connective tissue cells (Figure 5H and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5H and J.

claim: Progenitors that bifurcate to myogenic and non-myogenic cell fates are present only in neural-crest depleted regions.
source: These observations indicate that progenitors that bifurcate to myogenic and non-myogenic cell fates are present only in neural-crest depleted regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings described in the text.

claim: This property is associated primarily with Myf5 expression, as subsequent activation of Myod within this lineage appears to lock cell fate into the myogenic program and suppress their connective tissue potential.
source: This property is associated primarily with Myf5 expression, as subsequent activation of Myod within this lineage appears to lock cell fate into the myogenic program and suppress their connective tissue potential (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings described in the text and shown in Figure 5K.

claim: All stages contributed relatively equally to each 'GO Molecular Function' and 'Reactome pathways' terms despite their relatively diverse gene expression signatures.
source: We found that all stages contributed relatively equally to each 'GO Molecular Function' and 'Reactome pathways' terms despite their relatively diverse gene expression signatures (Figure 6D–E', Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6D-E' and supplementary figures.

claim: These non-myogenic cells are relatively homogeneous in gene signatures throughout cranial muscles.
source: This suggests that these non-myogenic cells are relatively homogeneous in gene signatures throughout cranial muscles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene set enrichment analysis findings.

claim: Foxp2, Hmga2, Meis1, Meox2, and Tcf7l2 were identified in all four scRNAseq datasets as key driver regulators.
source: Notably, Foxp2, Hmga2, Meis1, Meox2, and Tcf7l2 were identified in all four scRNAseq datasets as key driver regulators, and thus are likely to play significant role in the non-myogenic transition (Figure 7A, Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by driver regulator analysis shown in Figure 7A and Table 2.

claim: The Myf5-derived EOM cells expressed a relatively high level of Foxp2 compared to mandible and trunk muscles at E12.5.
source: FOXP2 immunostaining on Myf5Cre/+;Rosa26TdTom/+;PdgfraH2BGFP/+ E12.5 embryos showed that the Myf5-derived EOM cells expressed a relatively high level of Foxp2 compared to mandible and trunk muscles, consistent with their apparent high contribution to connective tissue (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: FACS analysis identified non-FAPs cells (GFPlow) transitioning towards a Pdgfra+ state in head and trunk regions but very few in the limb.
source: This analysis identified non-FAPs cells (GFPlow) transitioning towards a Pdgfra+ state in head and trunk regions but very few in the limb (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Trunk muscles presented the largest portion of transitioning cells (40%), while a similar transitioning population was noted in the head (20%) despite a large contribution of NCC to head connective tissues.
source: Interestingly, while trunk muscles presented the largest portion of transitioning cells (40%), a similar transitioning population was noted in the head (20%) despite a large contribution of NCC to head connective tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis data described in the text.

claim: Cardiopharyngeal mesoderm may have a superior potential to give rise to connective tissue compared to somite-derived progenitors in the limb (1.5%).
source: Thus, cardiopharyngeal mesoderm may have a superior potential to give rise to connective tissue compared to somite-derived progenitors in the limb (1.5%).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FACS analysis findings.

claim: Axin2 levels were elevated in the non-myogenic portion of all the different datasets.
source: Interestingly, Axin2 levels were elevated in the non-myogenic portion of all the different datasets (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Dkk2 was found to be elevated in non-myogenic cells, indicative of a putative positive-feedback loop mechanism supporting the maintenance of this population.
source: Additionally, Dkk2, which has been described as an activator of Wnt/β-cat pathway in the neural crest (Devotta et al., 2018), was also found to be elevated, indicative of a putative positive-feedback loop mechanism supporting the maintenance of this population.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Brown adipocytes, neurons, pericytes, and rib cartilage have been reported to express Myf5 in ancestral cells.
source: Brown adipocytes, neurons, pericytes, and rib cartilage have been reported to express Myf5 in ancestral cells (Daubas et al., 2000; Haldar et al., 2008; Sebo et al., 2018; Stuelsatz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When Myf5 expression is disrupted, cells can acquire non-myogenic fates and contribute to connective tissue, cartilage, and dermis.
source: Interestingly, when Myf5 expression is disrupted, cells can acquire non-myogenic fates and contribute to connective tissue (this study), cartilage, and dermis (Tajbakhsh et al., 1996), while others remain apparently undifferentiated (cells labeled with an asterisk in Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from this study and citations to previous literature.

claim: Myf5-expression alone is not sufficient to promote robust myogenic fate in multiple regions of developing embryos.
source: These studies suggest that Myf5-expression alone is not sufficient to promote robust myogenic fate in multiple regions of developing embryos.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from this study and previous literature.

claim: Myod+ cells do not contribute to rib cartilage and give rise to few connective tissue cells in the periocular and back regions.
source: Consistent with these observations, Myod+ cells do not contribute to rib cartilage (Wood et al., 2020) and give rise to few connective tissue cells in the periocular and back regions (this study).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from this study and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Myf5-expressing cells contribute to non-myogenic cells from early embryonic stages (E10.5) and continue to do so in the fetus.
source: We note that Myf5-expressing cells contribute to non-myogenic cells from early embryonic stages (E10.5) and continue to do so in the fetus, indicating that these bipotent cells persist well after muscles are established.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: Tcf4/Tcf7l2 was identified as a master regulator of fibroblastic fate during muscle-associated connective tissue development.
source: Tcf4/Tcf7l2 was identified as a master regulator of fibroblastic fate during muscle-associated connective tissue development, although it is also expressed in myogenic progenitors at lower levels (Kardon et al., 2003; Mathew et al., 2011; Sefton and Kardon, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Six2, Meox2, Egr2, and Foxs1 have been linked to skin fibroblast fates, and their repression favors a myofibroblastic potential.
source: Other transcription factors have been linked to skin fibroblast fates including Tcf4, Six2, Meox2, Egr2, and Foxs1, and their repression favors a myofibroblastic potential (Noizet et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Prrx1 was differentially expressed in the connective tissue population at various stages.
source: Interestingly, Prrx1, a marker for lateral plate mesoderm (Durland et al., 2008), was differentially expressed in the connective tissue population at various stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The differentiation of fetal myoblasts is inhibited by growth factors Tgfβ and Bmp4.
source: For example, the differentiation of fetal myoblasts is inhibited by growth factors Tgfβ and Bmp4 (Cossu et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Epha7 signaling is active in embryonic and adult myocytes and promotes their differentiation.
source: Epha7 signaling is active in embryonic and adult myocytes and promotes their differentiation (Arnold et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pdgf ligands emanating from hypaxial myogenic cells under the control of Myf5 were shown to be necessary for rib cartilage development.
source: Pdgf ligands emanating from hypaxial myogenic cells under the control of Myf5 were shown to be necessary from rib cartilage development (Tallquist et al., 2000; Vinagre et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pdgfra promotes expansion of fibroblasts during fibrosis.
source: Additionally, Pdgfra promotes expansion of fibroblasts during fibrosis (Olson and Soriano, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pdgfa expression was reduced in cells expressing high levels of Myog at the fetal stage.
source: Interestingly, we found that Pdgfa expression was reduced in cells expressing high levels of Myog at the fetal stage (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Cranial muscle development relies on the expression of Wnt and Bmp inhibitors from surrounding tissues.
source: Moreover, unlike trunk myogenesis, cranial muscle development relies on the expression of Wnt and Bmp inhibitors from surrounding tissues (Tzahor et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The Myf5-derived non-myogenic cells express Bmp4, Dkk2, and Axin2.
source: Interestingly, we showed that the Myf5-derived non-myogenic cells express Bmp4, Dkk2, and Axin2.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis described in the text.

claim: The Wnt effector complex Tcf/Lef is expressed to a lower extent in Myf5-derived non-myogenic cells.
source: Additionally, we showed that the Wnt effector complex Tcf/Lef is expressed to a lower extent in these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis described in the text.

claim: Another study suggested shared fate relationships between fibroblast connective tissue cells and skeletal muscle where fibroblastic cells commit to myogenic fate during limb development.
source: Of note, another study suggested shared fate relationships between fibroblast connective tissue cells and skeletal muscle where fibroblastic cells commit to myogenic fate during limb development (Esteves de Lima et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RNA velocity analysis did not reveal transitioning cells from non-myogenic clusters to myogenic even at early stages.
source: First, RNA velocity analysis did not reveal transitioning cells from non-myogenic clusters to myogenic (even at early stages), nor do they express myogenic markers.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings from RNA velocity analysis in this study.

claim: At least some of the non-myogenic cells gave rise to chondrocytes.
source: Further, at least some of these non-myogenic cells gave rise to chondrocytes, which to our knowledge has never been shown to give rise to skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings from this study.

claim: Bipotency appears to be more associated with myogenic cells since they express Myf5, and to a minor extent Myod.
source: Additionally, bipotency appears to be more associated with myogenic cells since they express Myf5, and to a minor extent Myod.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from this study.

claim: No NCC-derived Myf5+ cells were observed indicating that connective tissue in the head does not give rise to muscle.
source: Finally, we did not observe NCC-derived Myf5+ cells indicating that connective tissue in the head does not give rise to muscle.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings from this study.
